title: Given an array of `n` integers in the range `1` to `n` where some numbers appear once and some appear exactly twice, return all the numbers that appear twice, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (the output list excluded).
shortTitle: Find all Duplicate Numbers (Every Value Appearing Twice in 1..n)

s1_definition.profdef: This is the dual of find-all-missing. After placing each value `v` at index `v-1` with the duplicate-safe guard, any slot whose stored value does not equal `index+1` holds a value that was duplicated elsewhere; collecting those stored values yields all duplicates.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India expects one receipt per numbered slot 1 to n, but some receipts were printed twice. A clerk files each receipt in its matching slot; whatever receipt is still stranded in a wrong slot at the end is a receipt that got printed an extra time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Place `v` at index `v-1`; every stranded value where `value != index+1` is a duplicate.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is the dual of find-all-missing. After placing each value `v` at index `v-1` with the duplicate-safe guard, any slot whose stored value does not equal `index+1` holds a value that was duplicated elsewhere; collecting those stored values yields all duplicates.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India expects one receipt per numbered slot 1 to n, but some receipts were printed twice. A clerk files each receipt in its matching slot; whatever receipt is still stranded in a wrong slot at the end is a receipt that got printed an extra time.

**One line to remember:** Place `v` at index `v-1`; every stranded value where `value != index+1` is a duplicate.

sections.s2_technical:
The placement loop uses the same value-comparison guard as find-all-missing so duplicates do not cause infinite swaps. After the pass, each slot ideally holds `index+1`; wherever it does not, the stored value is one that appeared twice, because its second copy pushed another number out and itself could not reach its home. The scan is `if (nums[i] != i+1) result.add(nums[i]);` — note it collects the stored value, not `i+1`, which is the key difference from the missing-numbers scan.

For example `int[] receipts = {4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1};` after placement has indices where the stored value is not `index+1`, and those stored values are 2 and 3, the two duplicated receipts.

A senior-level nuance is the symmetry: on the exact same array, scanning for `i+1` gives the missing numbers and scanning for `nums[i]` gives the duplicates. The negative-marking alternative flips the sign of the element at index `abs(v)-1` and reports `v` when it finds the sign already negative; it is equally O(n)/O(1) but, unlike Cyclic Sort, cannot answer the missing-numbers question in the same pass.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India prints transaction receipts numbered 1 to n for a settlement window, and a printer fault occasionally emits a receipt twice. Finance must list every receipt number that was printed twice so the duplicates can be voided before the window closes, and the batches are too large to afford a second counting array. This is exactly find-all-duplicates: file each receipt at its home index, and every receipt left stranded in a wrong slot is one that was printed an extra time.

The code contains a `ReceiptAuditor` with `findDuplicateReceipts(int[])` and a demo over a faulty print run.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: `printed = {4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1}`, n=8.

Step 1: Placement sends 4 to index 3, 7 to index 6, 8 to index 7, 1 to index 0, and settles the single-occurrence numbers at their homes. When the duplicate 2 and duplicate 3 try to swap into homes already holding 2 and 3, the value guard advances the pointer instead of looping.

Step 2: After the pass, two slots cannot hold their proper `index+1` because the duplicates occupy the array where the missing numbers should be. Those two slots store the values 2 and 3.

Step 3: The scan collects the stored values 2 and 3 as the duplicates.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Printed receipt numbers: [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Receipts printed twice: [3, 2]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: printed = [4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1]  (1..8, some twice)
    │
    ▼
  ReceiptAuditor.findDuplicateReceipts()
    │ cyclic place (value-guard)
    │ scan: collect printed[idx] where printed[idx] ≠ idx+1
    ▼
  Output: [3, 2]  — receipts printed twice
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding all the numbers that appear twice in an array over the range one to n is the mirror image of finding all the missing numbers, and I solve both with the same Cyclic Sort placement loop. I place each value at the index equal to the value minus one, using the value-comparison swap guard so duplicates do not trap the pointer in an infinite swap. After that single pass, every slot that does not hold its proper index-plus-one is stranded because a duplicate crowded it out, and the value actually sitting in that stranded slot is a duplicate, so I collect the stored values rather than the indices.

The elegant part, and the thing I emphasize to an interviewer, is that on the identical array one scan for index-plus-one yields the missing numbers while another scan for the stored value yields the duplicates. That dual nature is why I prefer Cyclic Sort over the negative-marking trick, which can only answer one of the two questions per pass.

In my project at the National Bank of India this audited receipt print runs. The printer occasionally emitted a numbered receipt twice, and finance needed the full list of double-printed receipt numbers to void them before the settlement window closed, with batches too large for a second counting array. Placing each receipt at its home index and reporting the stranded stored values produced that list in linear time and constant extra space.
